Aviation: Your practice passenger count differs from the boarding list. What comes first?
A checked count matters more than a quick sign-off.
A training flight's weather briefing is out of date. What should the team use?
An updated briefing and instructor review
The exercise needs current conditions and qualified supervision.
The simulator reports an intermittent fault. What belongs in the handover?
Its symptoms, timing and unresolved status
A guess presented as a repair
An honest fault record lets the next qualified person investigate.
Beauty: A practice client describes a style using an unclear photo. What should you agree first?
A clear consultation prevents a mismatch before work starts.
The training colour chart lists a product restriction. What should your plan do?
Respect the restriction and ask the instructor
Ignore it for a brighter result
Product limits remain part of a supervised practice plan.
A mannequin exercise did not match the planned finish. What should you record?
The steps, result and needed adjustment
Recording the actual result makes the next practice useful.
Business: A client wants both a low price and extra work. What belongs in your proposal?
Separate scope, price and optional extras
Unlimited work for the first price
A clear scope makes the agreement workable.
Your model earns a profit but customers pay two months later. What must you check?
Cash available before bills fall due
Profit and cash timing are different constraints.
A pilot service gained customers but missed its deadline. What is a useful review?
A viable service needs customers and dependable delivery.
Care: A supervised care exercise includes a person's usual routine. What should guide your plan?
The fastest identical routine for everyone
Care planning starts with the person and their agreed needs.
A practice visit has an unfinished task. What should the next worker receive?
A clear note of what remains
A claim that everything is done
An unfinished task needs an honest handover.
The exercise asks you to do something outside your training. What is appropriate?
Knowing your limits is part of reliable care.
Design: A mock building entrance works for some visitors but excludes others. What should the brief include?
Access needs before choosing the layout
Access requirements shape a useful design from the start.
Three testers struggle at the same step. What should you change first?
Repeated difficulty is evidence for a targeted design change.
Two teams use different drawing revisions. What prevents a mismatched handover?
A shared revision record prevents teams building different designs.
Education: Your lesson has many activities but no clear goal. What should you add?
An observable skill learners will practise
A clear learning goal gives practice and feedback a purpose.
A learner gives the right answer but cannot explain it. What is useful next?
A short explanation or worked example
An explanation helps distinguish understanding from a lucky answer.
Half the group finishes early and half needs help. What should your next plan include?
Different levels of support keep the shared goal accessible.
Energy: A training solar array produces less than the model predicts. What should you compare?
Comparable conditions make an output check meaningful.
The simulated service task requires an authorization you lack. What comes next?
A training exercise does not replace authorization for real equipment.
A proposed upgrade saves energy but has a high initial cost. What belongs in the report?
An honest comparison includes both cost and expected savings.
Engineering: Your prototype meets one requirement and fails another. What should the review show?
Both results against the agreed requirements
A success claim with no measurements
A prototype review should expose unresolved requirements.
A component passes once but fails on a repeat run. What should you do?
Record the variation and repeat controlled tests
Repeatability and conditions matter when interpreting tests.
A late design change affects two connected parts. What must be checked?
Both interfaces and the affected tests
Connected parts require a coordinated change review.
Environment: Your mock river survey samples only one convenient point. What is missing?
A single larger sample at the same point
A survey needs a defensible sampling plan.
The training waste totals do not match the collection records. What should you check?
Consistent units and complete entries make an audit usable.
A local project improves one measure but worsens another. What should you publish?
Environmental trade-offs belong in the public record.
Facilities: A practice repair request says only 'broken'. What information is useful?
A completion date with no inspection
A clear work order helps schedule the right response.
Your training inventory includes unopened and partly used supplies. How should you count them?
Usable quantities prevent false stock forecasts.
An inspection leaves one fault unresolved. What should the record say?
Its status and the planned next step
An open fault needs a visible next step.
Finance: Your mock bank balance differs from the ledger. What should you compare first?
Reconciliation follows the records instead of forcing a matching total.
A forecast assumes every customer pays on time. What would improve it?
A second scenario makes cash risk visible.
Someone edits an earlier expense in your practice accounts. What should remain?
The original entry and dated correction
A traceable correction preserves the audit trail.
Food: Your practice order has a stated dietary restriction. What must the plan respect?
The stated restriction is part of the order requirements.
Three dishes finish at different times in a simulated service. What helps?
A schedule coordinates the service instead of relying on luck.
Your training kitchen wastes more stock than expected. What should you review?
Waste review needs both demand and usage records.
Government: Two practice applications have different deadlines. How should the queue be organized?
The applicant with the nicest letter
A public queue should follow defensible rules.
A draft service change misses a group it will affect. What should happen?
Affected people need a chance to inform the decision.
Your mock committee rejects an application. What should its record contain?
The reason and available review route
An invented reason after the meeting
A clear decision supports accountability and review.
Healthcare: Two simulated patient records have similar names. What comes first?
Check the required identifiers with the supervisor
Reliable identification comes before working on a record.
A classroom scenario asks for a decision beyond your qualification. What should you do?
Classroom evidence does not confer a clinical qualification.
Your simulated shift ends before a planned review. What should be handed over?
The pending review and relevant observations
A claim that the review happened
The next qualified team needs the actual pending work.
Hospitality: Your practice bookings allocate one room twice. What should you do?
Check availability and agree an honest alternative
Promise the room to both guests
A booking conflict needs a verified and agreed solution.
A guest asks for an adjustment outside the usual package. What should you clarify?
Clear terms prevent a service promise becoming a dispute.
A later shift must finish a guest's unresolved request. What should your briefing include?
The request, agreement and next step
A clear handover preserves the actual service commitment.
Legal: Two statements place an event on different dates. What should your practice timeline show?
A useful chronology distinguishes evidence from assumptions.
A mock contract has an undefined payment term. What should you flag?
The ambiguity and need for clarification
Unclear terms should be raised before agreement.
Your supervised case exercise has no decision yet. What should the update say?
Current status and the pending next step
An honest update separates progress from a promised outcome.
Logistics: A route model arrives after a customer's agreed window. What must you revise?
The route or an agreed delivery time
The recorded arrival without changing the route
The plan must fit the actual service agreement.
Your mock warehouse count is lower than the system balance. What should you investigate?
Stock reconciliation needs the movement records.
A proposed shipment exceeds vehicle capacity. What is workable?
Split the load or arrange suitable capacity
Record a smaller load without changing it
A delivery plan must respect capacity constraints.
Media: A practice article relies on an unnamed claim. What should happen before publication?
Publication needs an honest account of source strength.
The editor requests a change that alters the speaker's meaning. What should you do?
Raise the mismatch and preserve the meaning
An edit should not misrepresent its subject.
Your mock release contains an image from an unknown source. What needs checking?
The release record should establish where its assets came from.
Military: A training exercise assigns an unclear role. What should you request?
The objective, role and reporting line
A clear briefing helps the exercise stay coordinated.
A practice equipment return is missing one recorded item. What belongs in the register?
No entry for the missing item
The register must reflect the actual return.
Your simulated team completed the task but missed a safety check. What should be reviewed?
Both completion and the missed check
A debrief should expose process failures as well as results.
Office: Two practice meetings need the same room. What should you check?
Only the first name on each list
A mock caller needs a team you do not know. What should you do?
Check the directory and confirm the handover
A checked handover is more useful than a confident guess.
A practice form has an incorrect address. How should it be corrected?
Verify the address and record the correction
Verified corrections preserve a usable office record.
Public Safety: A simulated incident report omits its location. What should you request first?
The location and verified incident details
A useful incident brief needs reliable facts.
A training plan assigns the same crew to two exercises at once. What must change?
A team cannot be allocated beyond its actual capacity.
Your exercise ends with an unresolved concern. What should the review include?
An unresolved concern needs a recorded owner and next step.
Recreation: Your practice activity has beginners and experienced participants. What helps?
A session should fit the participants and supervision available.
A mock activity has more bookings than supervised spaces. What should you do?
Arrange capacity or agree another session
Change the count on paper only
Supervised capacity is a real constraint.
Feedback says the activity was enjoyable but hard to follow. What should improve?
Enjoyment and understandable instructions both matter.
Retail: A practice item's shelf price differs from the system. What should you check?
The current verified price and correction process
A price discrepancy needs a checked correction.
Your training shelves mix earlier and later deliveries. What should you use?
Rotation follows the product's actual stock requirements.
A mock return lacks the original receipt. What should you consult?
The published return policy and available evidence
A consistent return process uses policy and evidence.
Science: Your experiment has no comparison condition. What should the design add?
A suitable control and recorded variables
More copies of the same uncontrolled run
A control helps interpret what caused the observed difference.
One training result differs greatly from the others. What should you do?
Keep the record and investigate conditions
Unexpected observations need investigation rather than erasure.
Your small study supports a limited finding. What should the conclusion say?
The finding and limits of the evidence
A defensible conclusion stays within its evidence.
Security: A practice visitor lacks the required authorization. What should you check?
The access rules and authorized contact
Access decisions follow authorization rather than appearances.
Two witnesses disagree in a simulated incident. What should you record?
Both accounts and what you observed
A useful record separates accounts from direct observations.
Your practice patrol has one check still outstanding. What belongs in the handover?
The unfinished check and next step
A handover should make unfinished work visible.
Tech: A mock app fails only after a particular sequence. What should the report include?
The steps, expected result and actual result
A guessed cause with no steps
Reproducible steps let another person investigate the same failure.
A feature works alone but breaks an older workflow. What should be checked?
The feature and the affected existing paths
Testing should include interactions with existing behavior.
Your training release has a known unresolved defect. What should the notes state?
Its effect and any verified workaround
A claim that no defects remain
A release record should describe the actual delivered behavior.
Trades: A simulated repair request has no measurements. What should you establish?
The exercise needs a measured specification.
A training replacement fits physically but has a different rating. What should you do?
Check the specification with the instructor
Physical fit alone does not establish suitability.
Your mock repair has not been checked against its brief. What comes before sign-off?
Only a photo of the part
Sign-off needs evidence that the agreed checks were completed.
Transport: Your practice route ignores loading time. What should the estimate include?
The shortest line on the map
A delivery estimate includes the whole job.
A mock vehicle is scheduled for service during a delivery. What should you arrange?
A suitable alternative or revised booking
Scheduling must reflect the vehicle's actual availability.
A simulated delivery reaches a different person than agreed. What should be verified?
The approved recipient and delivery record
A delivery record needs a verified handover.
